## 1. Load the processed data

```{r load}
# Open the project's .Rproj file before running chunks.
# Install psych once in the Console if needed: install.packages("psych")
#install.packages("psych")
library(psych)

h1Data <- read.csv("Data/processed_data/project_h1.csv")
h2Data <- read.csv("Data/processed_data/project_h2.csv")

```

## 2. Look at the distribution first

```{r histogram}
# A histogram groups numerical values into intervals (bins).
# Bar height shows how many observations fall in each interval.
# Start by looking at the distribution before calculating summary statistics.
hist(h1Data$infmoral_sex)
hist(h1Data$infmoral_emo)
hist(h2Data$jealsex)
hist(h2Data$appearTime)

# Add readable labels to the same histogram.
hist(h1Data$infmoral_sex,
     main="Distribution of moral wrongness of sexual infidelity",
     xlab="Moral wrongness of sexual infidelity (1-7)")
hist(h1Data$infmoral_emo,
     main="Distribution of moral wrongness of emotional infidelity",
     xlab="Moral wrongness of emotional infidelity (1-7)")
hist(h2Data$jealsex,
     main="Distribution of jealousy about partner's sexual infidelity",
     xlab="Jealousy about partner's sexual infidelity (1-7)")
hist(h2Data$appearTime,
     main="Distribution of daily appearance time",
     xlab="Daily time spent enhancing appearance (minutes)")
```

## 3. One statistic at a time

```{r individual_statistics}
# Mean: add the scores and divide by the number of observed responses.
mean(h1Data$infmoral_sex, na.rm = TRUE)
mean(h1Data$infmoral_emo, na.rm = TRUE)
mean(h2Data$appearTime, na.rm = TRUE)
mean(h2Data$jealsex, na.rm = TRUE)

# Median: the middle score after sorting the responses.
median(h1Data$infmoral_sex, na.rm = TRUE)
median(h1Data$infmoral_emo, na.rm = TRUE)
median(h2Data$appearTime, na.rm = TRUE)
median(h2Data$jealsex, na.rm = TRUE)

# Table: count how many people are in each category.
table(h1Data$raisedFrance, useNA = "ifany")
# Range: return the minimum and maximum, rather than their difference.
range(h1Data$infmoral_sex, na.rm = TRUE)
range(h1Data$infmoral_emo, na.rm = TRUE)
range(h2Data$appearTime, na.rm = TRUE)
range(h2Data$jealsex, na.rm = TRUE)

# IQR: the 75th percentile minus the 25th percentile.
IQR(h1Data$infmoral_sex, na.rm = TRUE)
IQR(h1Data$infmoral_emo, na.rm = TRUE)
IQR(h2Data$appearTime, na.rm = TRUE)
IQR(h2Data$jealsex, na.rm = TRUE)
```

## 4. Standardize a variable

```{r standardize}
# scale() uses z = (original score - mean) / standard deviation by default.
# Keep the original commitment scores and store the standardized values separately.
# scale() returns a matrix; as.numeric() makes a simple numeric column.
h1Data$infmoral_sex_z <- scale(h1Data$infmoral_sex)
h1Data$infmoral_emo_z <- scale(h1Data$infmoral_emo)
h2Data$appearTime_z <- scale(h2Data$appearTime)
h2Data$jealsex_z <- scale(h2Data$jealsex)

# Standardized scores have mean approximately 0 and standard deviation 1.
mean(h1Data$infmoral_sex_z, na.rm=TRUE)
sd(h1Data$infmoral_sex_z, na.rm=TRUE)
mean(h1Data$infmoral_emo_z, na.rm=TRUE)
sd(h1Data$infmoral_emo_z, na.rm=TRUE)
mean(h2Data$appearTime_z, na.rm=TRUE)
sd(h2Data$appearTime_z, na.rm=TRUE)
mean(h2Data$jealsex_z, na.rm=TRUE)
sd(h2Data$jealsex_z, na.rm=TRUE)

```

## 5. Covariance and correlation

```{r association}
# Covariance describes whether two variables tend to move together.
# Positive: higher values tend to occur together. Negative: higher values tend to accompany lower values.
# Its size depends on the units and is not restricted to -1 through 1.
cov(h1Data$infmoral_sex, h1Data$infmoral_emo, use="complete.obs")
cov(h2Data$appearTime, h2Data$jealsex, use="complete.obs")

# Pearson correlation expresses a linear association on a -1 to 1 scale.
cor(h1Data$infmoral_sex, h1Data$infmoral_emo, use="complete.obs")
cor(h2Data$appearTime, h2Data$jealsex, use="complete.obs")

# Select numerical variables only; do not include participant IDs or category codes.
corData1 <- h1Data[, c("infmoral_sex", "infmoral_emo")]
corData2 <- h2Data[, c("appearTime", "jealsex")]

# A correlation matrix gives the correlation for each pair of columns.
cor(corData1, use="complete.obs")
cor(corData2, use="complete.obs")
# The diagonal is 1 because each variable is correlated with itself.
```

## 6. Several statistics at once

```{r combined_summaries}
# summary() reports minimum, quartiles, median, mean, maximum, and missing counts when present.
summary(corData1)
summary(corData2)

# psych::describe() reports n, mean, SD, median, minimum, maximum, range width (max minus min), skewness, kurtosis, and other summaries.
# However it does not report every statistic above: compute IQR, cov(), and cor() separately.
psych::describe(corData1)
psych::describe(corData2)
```
